# Near-Miss {#sec-imbalenced-nearmiss}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Near-Miss
:::

The NearMiss method is a method that is used to remove observations from the majority classes [@mani2003nearmiss].
Like with many of the other methods in this section,
we are going to focus on points based on their distance to instances of other classes.

What we are doing is that we are removing points from the majority class that are far away from the minority class.
We are keeping points from the majority class that are close to the minority class.
In other words, we are only keeping the "near misses".
While the idea is fairly straightforward,
it has 3 different recognized variants based on how we define a near miss.

-   **NearMiss-1**: Selects majority class observations with the smallest average distance to the three **closest** minority class observations.
-   **NearMiss-2**: Selects majority class observations with the smallest average distance to the three **furthest** minority class observations.
-   **NearMiss-3**: It is a two-stage method, first for each minority class, their nearest neighbors are kept, and then we select the majority class observations with the smallest distance to each minority class observation.

While the distinction between the 1 and 2 variants might seem small,
what you are getting is that with NearMiss-1, you are preserving samples that are most similar to the minority class,
and with NearMiss-2, you are preserving samples that are least similar to the minority class.
NearMiss-3 is trying to have a more blended selection.

This method, like many of the other methods, is technically not restricted to be used on the majority class,
and could, in theory, be used on any number of classes in the data set.

One of the convenient things about this method is that it technically works by giving the observations an ordering,
And we just have to find the cut point that determines how many points to retain.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_nearmiss()`, and the `version` argument selects which of the three variants to use.

```{r}
#| label: step_nearmiss
nearmiss_res <- recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_nearmiss(MS_Zoning, version = 1) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

nearmiss_res |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

Unlike [Tomek link removal](imbalenced-tomek.qmd), this method does give you a target to aim at.
The majority class was brought all the way down to the size of the minority class, and `under_ratio` adjusts how far it goes.

The three variants all return the same number of observations, since the count is set by `under_ratio` rather than by the data.
What changes is which observations are kept.

```{r}
#| label: step_nearmiss-versions
nearmiss_version <- function(version) {
  recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
    step_nearmiss(MS_Zoning, version = version) |>
    prep() |>
    bake(new_data = NULL) |>
    filter(MS_Zoning == "Residential_Low_Density") |>
    summarise(version = version, mean_lot_area = mean(Lot_Area), mean_year = mean(Year_Built))
}

bind_rows(nearmiss_version(1), nearmiss_version(2), nearmiss_version(3))
```

The three variants keep noticeably different parts of the majority class, which is what the description above would lead us to expect.

## Python Examples

```{python}
#| label: python-setup
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
from sklearn import set_config

set_config(transform_output="pandas")
pd.set_option('display.precision', 3)
```

We are using the same subset of the `ames` data set as above.

```{python}
#| label: show-data-py
from feazdata import ames

ames_imbalance = ames[ames["MS_Zoning"].isin(
    ["Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density"])]

X = ames_imbalance[["Lot_Area", "Year_Built", "Gr_Liv_Area", "Full_Bath"]]
y = ames_imbalance["MS_Zoning"]

y.value_counts()
```

{imblearn} provides `NearMiss()`, with the same `version` argument.

```{python}
#| label: nearmiss
from imblearn.under_sampling import NearMiss

X_res, y_res = NearMiss(version=1).fit_resample(X, y)

y_res.value_counts()
```

And the same comparison across the three variants.

```{python}
#| label: nearmiss-versions
import pandas as pd

rows = []
for version in [1, 2, 3]:
    X_res, y_res = NearMiss(version=version).fit_resample(X, y)
    kept = X_res[y_res == "Residential_Low_Density"]
    rows.append({
        "version": version,
        "mean_lot_area": kept["Lot_Area"].mean(),
        "mean_year": kept["Year_Built"].mean(),
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

Comparing the two tables, versions 1 and 3 agree closely across the implementations while version 2 does not.
This is not a disagreement about the algorithm, it is a difference in defaults.
{themis} uses `neighbors = 5` and {imblearn} uses `n_neighbors = 3`.
Version 2 measures distance to the *furthest* neighbors, so it is far more sensitive to that number than the other two variants, which look at the closest ones.
Setting `neighbors = 3` in {themis} reproduces the {imblearn} result exactly.

It is worth taking this as a general warning rather than a fact about this one method.
Two implementations of the same published algorithm will frequently disagree on defaults, and the disagreement is easiest to miss precisely where it matters most.
